items.title: Almost no professional forecaster saw 2008 coming
items.claim: After the 2008 financial crisis, the Queen famously asked LSE economists why no one saw it coming. What's the accurate picture?

options.text: Most leading economists predicted the crisis from the early 2000s
A small number of analysts (Raghuram Rajan, Nouriel Roubini, Steve Keen, Brooksley Born, Michael Burry) warned about systemic risk; the consensus, including the IMF and most central banks, did not
The IMF published a precise prediction in 2006
The crisis was a complete surprise that no one anywhere foresaw

items.reveal:
Rajan's 2005 Jackson Hole paper ('Has Financial Development Made the World Riskier?') was dismissed by Larry Summers. Roubini was nicknamed 'Dr Doom' for warnings from 2006. Steve Keen had modelled private debt dynamics. Michael Burry famously bet against subprime (Big Short). The Bank for International Settlements raised flags.

Macroeconomic models in use (DSGE) had no banking sector and no default. The Queen's 2008 question to LSE got a follow-up letter (2009) from leading British economists admitting a 'failure of the collective imagination of many bright people... to understand the risks to the system as a whole.'
items.why: Economics' forecasting record isn't great — but the deeper issue was that mainstream models couldn't even represent the relevant risks. Heterodoxy isn't always wrong.

items.title: FDI flows have plateaued since 2015
items.claim: Global Foreign Direct Investment flows reached record highs in the 2000s. UNCTAD data from 2020 onwards shows what pattern?

options.text: FDI flows have plateaued and partially fragmented along geopolitical lines (US-EU vs China-aligned blocs); 'slowbalisation' or 'fracturing globalisation' is the now-common framing
All FDI is now in the metaverse

items.reveal:
UNCTAD World Investment Report data: global FDI peaked at $2 trillion in 2015; 2022 flows were $1.3 trillion. Trade as a share of global GDP also flattened.

Drivers: US-China trade tensions (tariffs from 2018), COVID supply-chain reshoring, geopolitical fragmentation (Russia-Ukraine, Taiwan strait), reshoring/nearshoring policies (US CHIPS Act, EU Chips Act, IRA).

The 'end of history' globalisation narrative of the 1990s-2000s has been substantially complicated.
items.why: Globalisation is not a one-way ratchet. The political economy of trade and investment has shifted in ways that affect macroeconomic forecasting and corporate strategy.

items.title: Natural monopolies have decreasing average costs
items.claim: Water supply, electricity distribution and rail track are often described as natural monopolies. What's the defining feature?

options.text: High fixed costs and economies of scale that extend across the entire market — so a single firm produces at lower average cost than competing firms; competition wastes resources duplicating infrastructure

items.reveal:
UK utility privatisations (1980s-90s) separated naturally monopolistic infrastructure (electricity grids, water distribution, rail track) from contestable elements (generation, supply, train operating companies) and regulated the former.

Ofwat (water 1989), Ofgem (energy 1986), Office of Rail Regulation. RPI-X price controls (Stephen Littlechild's framework) were a UK innovation copied internationally.

New technologies (distributed solar, EVs) are testing whether parts of utility networks remain natural monopolies.
items.why: Market structure isn't only about firm decisions; it reflects cost characteristics. Regulating natural monopolies needs different tools from policing competition.
